title: Thanksgiving
hook: in North America, a harvest thanks at the table

segments.voice: Yesterday, servant king: a crown of thorns, and your line was a different king.

The ship has been driven by a storm for fourteen days. No sun, no stars. The cargo has gone over the side. The sailors have just been caught trying to slip away in the lifeboat. It's the dark before dawn, and nobody has eaten properly since the storm began. Then a prisoner, a tentmaker called Paul, takes a loaf and does something ordinary. He says grace. A strange place to begin a day about Thanksgiving, North America's harvest meal with thanks at the table. But that's where today starts.

In Acts, in the King James words, Paul urges them all to eat, and then "he took bread, and gave thanks to God in presence of them all: and when he had broken it, he began to eat." The storm isn't over; the ship hasn't reached land. He gives thanks in the middle, in front of terrified people, and then: "Then were they all of good cheer, and they also took some meat." One person's grace turned into everyone's breakfast. That grace has a pattern behind it. In Mark, with a hungry crowd in the wilderness, Jesus takes the loaves, gives thanks, breaks them, and gives them to his disciples to set before the people. In Luke, two friends at Emmaus only recognize the risen Jesus when he takes bread, blesses it and breaks it. More than once, the meal begins with thanks. A letter in Paul's name says: "For every creature of God is good, and nothing to be refused, if it be received with thanksgiving." Creature there means every created thing. The potatoes count. And to the church at Thessalonica, Paul wrote: "In every thing give thanks." Not for every thing, some readers point out. In every thing. In the storm, too. At a Thanksgiving table, grace changes from house to house: a psalm, "O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good: for his mercy endureth for ever," a grandmother's grace, or just hands held for a moment. The shape is the ship's: stop, give thanks out loud, then eat together.
screen: `JESUS TOOK THE LOAVES AND GAVE THANKS.`

segments.voice: Think of your next meal, and of one thing in your life still unsettled, a storm still going; don't try to solve it, just let it be there. Then choose a few plain words of thanks to say before that meal anyway. If you pray, use a grace your family knows, or the psalm's line, O give thanks unto the LORD; for he is good; if not, just choose the words, and the breath you'll pause for.
Thanksgiving. In North America, a harvest meal with thanks at the table. In the Bible, giving thanks in every thing, even in a storm.
Your line: for all good gifts. Thanks can come before the storm is over. That's day one thousand fifty-nine.

howItsDone: Some Christian families in the United States and Canada say grace before the Thanksgiving meal, sometimes holding hands, and some churches hold a Thanksgiving service or gather food for neighbors in need.

chat.says: Things at home are hard this year. How do we give thanks at Thanksgiving?
options: Paul gave thanks in the middle of a storm. Thanks can come before things are fixed.
Wait until things settle down; thanks only counts once the trouble is over.
Skip grace this year; the Bible only asks for thanks after a good harvest.
chat.meaning: Paul took bread and gave thanks before the storm was over, and wrote: in every thing give thanks. In the storm, too.

notes: Claims rule: no dates or origin story for Thanksgiving (1621, Lincoln's proclamation, Canada's October date) are given; the index hook supplies 'in North America, a harvest thanks at the table'.
Consider whether a brief, careful word belongs here about Native American experience of the holiday; left out of the voice as outside the cited text.

'Fourteen days' is Acts 27:33 ('the fourteenth day'); 'no sun, no stars' is Acts 27:20; cargo and tackle thrown out 27:18–19; sailors and the boat 27:30–32. Confirm the sequence and 'the dark before dawn' (27:33, 'while the day was coming on').
1 Timothy is described as 'a letter in Paul's name' to avoid an authorship claim. Confirm the Keeper is comfortable with this phrasing.
'Not for every thing, some readers point out. In every thing.' is now attributed to some readers.
'Creature there means every created thing' is a gloss on the KJV word. Confirm.
Carry 'for all good gifts' echoes day 1049 ('all good gifts'); the angle here is grace at the table, in an unsettled moment, rather than harvest produce.

Editor pass: the feeding scene moved from John 6 (the boy's loaves, used tomorrow for Andrew) to Mark 8:6, and the original word now cites Mark 8:6; 'Paul wasn't inventing anything. He was copying' (a claim about his intent) became 'Paul's grace has a pattern behind it'; 'again and again' softened to 'more than once'; the practice and carry no longer trace food back to the people who grew it (day 1049's practice) and instead give thanks in the middle of something unsettled, as Paul did.

Second editor pass: fork setup 'no food' changed to 'almost nobody has eaten' (Acts 27:33 says they had been fasting; 27:38 shows wheat still aboard); the stock line 'they're standing in a long line' cut, also to avoid anticipating day 1061's line image.

Audit pass: Paul 'stands up' (Acts 27:21, earlier speech) changed to 'speaks up' for the grace at 27:33–35; Mark 8:6 now says Jesus gave the loaves to his disciples to set before the people (not that he handed them out), in the teach, match and original note; the word segment no longer reduces thanksgiving to Paul's one grace.
